title: Crocheting over a cord
subtitle: Working crochet stitches around cotton rope or macramé cord for baskets and homewares
excerpt: Crocheting over a cord means working stitches around a length of rope or thick cotton cord rather than into a yarn foundation chain. The cord provides structure and bulk; the crochet thread wraps it, covering the surface and locking the cord into the finished shape.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776. Contemporary macramé and homeware crochet references.

glossaryTerms.definition: A technique in which crochet stitches are worked around a length of rope, cord, or clothesline rather than into a yarn chain, enclosing the cord inside each stitch to build a firm, structural fabric.
In cord crochet, joining each new ring of cord to the previous ring using crochet stitches, building a flat coiled mat or the walls of a basket.

content.text: is the technique for making baskets, mats, and bowls by wrapping crochet thread around rope or thick cotton cord. Instead of working into a yarn foundation, you work your stitches around the cord itself, enclosing it inside each stitch. The cord gives the piece its structure; the thread holds the coils together and covers the surface.

Common cord materials are 5 mm or 8 mm twisted cotton rope, waxed cotton cord, and clothesline. The thread is usually a fine cotton (size 10 crochet cotton or a DK-weight smooth cotton yarn) in a colour that contrasts with or matches the cord depending on the effect you want.

items.name: Cotton rope, 5 mm or 8 mm diameter
items.note: Twisted (not braided) cotton rope works best as it grips the thread. Avoid polypropylene rope, which is slippery.

items.name: DK cotton yarn or size 10 crochet cotton
items.note: Something smooth that wraps tightly. Textured yarns obscure the cord structure.

items.name: Crochet hook, 3.5 mm to 5 mm
items.note: Sized to the thread, not to the rope

items.name: Tapestry needle
items.note: For finishing off thread tails into the body of the piece

content.text: Leave a 15 cm tail of thread. Coil the end of the rope into a small flat ring, two loops around. The centre hole should be about 2 cm across.
Hold the coil flat in your non-dominant hand. Insert the hook through the centre hole, wrap the thread over the hook, and draw a loop through. Chain 1. This is the first stitch anchor.

Work double crochet (UK) stitches around the inner ring of cord, spacing them about 5 mm apart: insert the hook around the cord (not into it), wrap the thread, draw up a loop, yarn over, draw through two loops. Continue until the inner ring is covered.

: lay the next section of rope alongside the first ring. Work one double crochet (UK) around the new rope, then join it to the previous ring with one double crochet (UK) worked around both ropes at once. Alternate joining and free stitches as needed to keep the mat flat.

Continue coiling and joining, adding more stitches to the outer rings to compensate for the increasing circumference. A flat mat needs more stitches per ring as it grows; a bowl needs fewer, which causes the sides to curve upward.

To finish, cut the rope at an angle, taper the end with scissors or tape, and continue wrapping thread tightly over the tapered section until it is fully covered. Fasten off and thread the tail into the back of the piece with the tapestry needle.

items.symptom: The mat is curling upward at the edges instead of lying flat
items.cause: Not enough stitches are being added as the circumference of each ring increases.
items.fix: Add an extra joining stitch every 3 to 4 stitches on the outer rings. If the problem is severe, add a joining stitch every other stitch on the next full ring.

items.symptom: The thread is splitting the cord rather than wrapping around it
items.cause: The hook is being inserted into the body of the cord rather than encircling it.
items.fix: Insert the hook from underneath, going around the full diameter of the cord rather than between the twisted strands.

items.symptom: The finished piece feels floppy and does not hold its shape
items.cause: The stitches are too loose, or the rope is too fine relative to the thread.
items.fix: Tighten the working tension or move down a hook size. For a bowl that needs to hold its shape unsupported, choose a stiffer cord (8 mm twisted rope rather than 5 mm).

content.text: A flat mat about 20 cm in diameter makes a good first piece: small enough to finish quickly, large enough to see how the stitching sits. Once the coiling motion feels natural, switch to building walls for a bowl by reducing the stitch count on the outer rings, which causes the mat to curve upward rather than staying flat.
